points: Why is the southern kingdom punished more severely than the north? Yechezkel's parable: two daughters, Ahola and Aholiva, both promiscuous. Ahola is Shomron, the north - 'her tent,' a temple to foreign gods, or at least not one Hashem decreed. Aholiva is 'My tent is in her' - Yehuda, the people who have the Beis HaMikdash in Yerushalayim.

Ahola pursued the Assyrians, wanting to be like them and connect to them - some point to King Menachem ben Gadi, who sent money to Ashur to buy the alliance. The punchline: the very Assyrians she chased came, attacked, and carried her off into exile.

Aholiva saw her sister's fate and sinned anyway - worse, because she had the Beis HaMikdash, so much more inspiration, and still did not step it up. More opportunity for spiritual growth means more accountability: someone living in a city with the Mikdash, or in modern Israel, or in a generation witnessing quasi-miracles, carries a greater claim against them than those who saw less.

The severest critique targets inconsistency: the people committed idolatry, adultery and murder - the three sins the sages say destroyed the Beis HaMikdash - and on the very same day came to the Beis HaMikdash. Worse than religious versus irreligious is the person devoted to shul and learning whose actions flatly contradict the spirituality they are gaining; a society that normalizes that split is what Yechezkel is calling out.

Both kingdoms tried to become like the nations that ultimately destroyed them - the sin itself was the punishment. The same holds individually: chasing kavod, money or lust, the pursuit itself digs the grave. Punishment is so often not a lightning bolt from Hashem but man-made - our own poor choices about relationships, behavior and way of life causing our own pain.
